name: Zig
year_note: Andrew Kelley announced Zig on 8 February 2016. The language is still pre-1.0: each 0.x release (most recently 0.16.0, April 2026) can break source compatibility, so code — including the snippets here — targets a specific version.
tagline: A small, explicit systems language meant to improve on C: compile-time code execution, no hidden control flow, no hidden allocations.
summary: Zig is a general-purpose systems programming language designed as a pragmatic improvement on C. It has no macros, preprocessor, exceptions, operator overloading or hidden memory allocation; instead a single mechanism, `comptime`, runs ordinary Zig code at compile time to provide generics, conditional compilation and reflection. Its toolchain doubles as a C/C++ cross-compiler (`zig cc`), and its standard library passes allocators — and, since 0.16, I/O — as explicit parameters.
history:
Andrew Kelley announced Zig in February 2016 with the goal of a language 'more pragmatic than C'. He had been building a digital audio workstation and found Go's interoperability with C libraries difficult and its garbage collector a cause of audio delays, C++ prone to memory-corruption bugs that took weeks to fix, and Rust's rules hard to satisfy. The original compiler was written mainly in C++ on top of LLVM. Since 2020 development has been funded by the non-profit Zig Software Foundation through donations and corporate sponsorships.

A self-hosted compiler written in Zig became the default in 0.10 (2022), and the C++ implementation was removed in 0.11 (2023), replaced by a WebAssembly build of the compiler for bootstrapping; language-level async/await, which only the old compiler supported, was not carried over. In November 2025 the project moved from GitHub to Codeberg. Zig 0.16 (April 2026) made I/O an explicit interface (`std.Io`) with futures, cancellation and interchangeable threaded or evented back ends — an answer to the 'function colouring' problem — and deprecated the `@cImport` builtin in favour of C header translation through the build system. Although still pre-1.0, Zig is used in production by projects such as the TigerBeetle database and the Ghostty terminal emulator.
innovations: comptime: ordinary code evaluated by the compiler, unifying generics, conditional compilation and reflection without macros, templates or a preprocessor
Types as first-class compile-time values: a generic type is just a function that returns a type
No hidden control flow or hidden allocations: allocators are passed explicitly, and there are no operator overloads, exceptions or destructors
Error unions with try/catch/errdefer, and error return traces in safe builds
`zig cc`: a drop-in C/C++ compiler that cross-compiles to dozens of targets out of the box, bundling libc headers
Build modes that choose between checked safety (Debug, ReleaseSafe) and unchecked speed or size (ReleaseFast, ReleaseSmall)
I/O as an interface (0.16), letting the same code run on blocking or event-driven I/O without 'coloured' async functions

typing.notes: `const x = f();` infers local types. Integers may have any bit width (u3, i47) and conversions must be explicit unless lossless. Generic code is duck-typed at compile time: `anytype` parameters and comptime type arguments are checked per instantiation.

influenced_by.note: Designed as a better C for the same domain: C ABI, direct C interop, and a toolchain that also compiles C.
Listed by Wikipedia; comptime generics fill the role of templates without a separate template language.
Listed by Wikipedia; Kelley tried Go before starting Zig, and Zig's `defer` resembles Go's (Zig adds `errdefer`).
Listed by Wikipedia; Kelley found Rust's rules too hard to satisfy and chose a simpler route to safety (optionals, error unions, checked build modes).

influenced_by_external.name: LLVM IR
influenced_by_external.note: Listed by Wikipedia; Zig's first compiler targeted LLVM, and its arbitrary-width integers mirror LLVM's iN types.

structured-control.note: Labelled blocks and loops; `if`, `switch` and blocks are expressions.

tail-calls.note: `@call(.always_tail, f, args)` guarantees a tail call where the backend supports it (e.g. LLVM, not yet the self-hosted x86-64 backend).

exceptions.note: Error unions (`!T`): `try` propagates and `catch` handles errors, but they are ordinary return values, not unwinding exceptions; panics are unrecoverable.

pattern-matching.note: `switch` on tagged unions and enums is exhaustive with payload captures (`|r|`), but there is no nested destructuring.

type-inference.note: Local only; function signatures are explicit.

generics.note: Via comptime type parameters: functions take `comptime T: type` and may return new types.

option-types.note: `?T` optionals; ordinary pointers cannot be null.

abstract-data-types.note: Declarations are file-private unless `pub`, but struct fields are always public by design.

modules.note: Every file is a struct-namespace imported with @import; packages are declared in build.zig.zon.

first-class-functions.note: Function pointers and functions passed as comptime values; no closures or lambda syntax.

immutability.note: Parameters are immutable, and the compiler rejects a `var` that is never mutated, pushing code toward `const`.

pointers.note: Single-item, many-item and slice pointers; heap memory comes from an explicitly passed Allocator.

async-await.note: std.Io's io.async()/io.concurrent() return futures that are awaited or cancelled; the language-level async/await of the old C++ compiler was not carried over.

reflection.note: Compile-time only: @typeInfo, @field, @hasDecl and `inline for` over fields (how std.fmt prints any type).

compile-time-execution.note: `comptime` blocks, parameters and expressions run ordinary Zig in the compiler, with a configurable evaluation branch quota.

milestones.event: 0.10: the self-hosted compiler becomes the default
0.11: C++ implementation removed, WebAssembly-based bootstrap; experimental package manager
Development moves from GitHub to Codeberg (26 November)
0.16: I/O as an interface (std.Io), `std.process.Init` main; @cImport deprecated in favour of build-system C translation

trivia: The name was picked by a script that generated random combinations of letters starting with 'z'.
Zig grew out of Kelley's frustration while writing a digital audio workstation: Go's garbage collector caused audio delays, C++ produced memory-corruption bugs, and Rust's rules were hard to satisfy.

hello.notes: Since 0.16 all I/O goes through an explicit `std.Io` instance, which the 'juicy main' receives in `init.io`. Earlier versions wrote via `std.io.getStdOut()`, so Zig snippets are version-specific.

factorial.notes: Output goes through a buffered `std.Io.File.Writer` that must be flushed; the format string is parsed at compile time.

fizzbuzz.notes: `for (1..16) |i|` iterates a half-open range of usize values.

higher-order.notes: Zig has no closures or iterator adaptors, so an explicit loop is the idiomatic form.

shapes.notes: A tagged union (`union(enum)`) with an exhaustive `switch` and payload captures; methods are just functions declared inside the type.

signature.title: comptime: types as values
signature.notes: `Pair` runs at compile time and returns a new struct type — the same pattern as std.ArrayList(T) and every other Zig generic. `comptime fib(10)` is evaluated by the compiler; deeper recursion would need `@setEvalBranchQuota`.

toolchains.name: Zig (official tarball)
toolchains.install: apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl xz-utils && curl -L https://ziglang.org/download/0.16.0/zig-x86_64-linux-0.16.0.tar.xz | tar -xJ -C /opt && ln -s /opt/zig-x86_64-linux-0.16.0/zig /usr/local/bin/zig
toolchains.notes: No official Docker image; plw-zig is debian:trixie-slim plus the official 0.16.0 tarball, with a pre-warmed cache. Builds in Debug mode (safety checks on, self-hosted x86_64 backend): about 2 s per run against 9 s for ReleaseSafe, which goes through LLVM. The snippets use 0.16-only APIs (std.process.Init, std.Io) and will not compile on 0.15 or earlier.

runtime.notes: Pin the exact Zig version: the standard library changes between 0.x releases.
